claim: In the adult Drosophila midgut, basal intestinal stem cells give rise to enteroblasts that integrate into the epithelium as they differentiate into enterocytes.
source: In the adult Drosophila midgut, basal intestinal stem cells give rise to enteroblasts that integrate into the epithelium as they differentiate into enterocytes.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract describing the basic biological process studied in the manuscript.

claim: Integrating enteroblasts must generate a new apical domain and break through the septate junctions between neighbouring enterocytes, while maintaining barrier function.
source: Integrating enteroblasts must generate a new apical domain and break through the septate junctions between neighbouring enterocytes, while maintaining barrier function.
evidence: This describes the biological challenge that enteroblasts face during integration, based on the authors' observations.

claim: Enteroblasts form an apical membrane initiation site (AMIS) when they reach the septate junction between the enterocytes.
source: We observe that enteroblasts form an apical membrane initiation site (AMIS) when they reach the septate junction between the enterocytes.
evidence: This is a direct observation reported in the abstract and supported by imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Cadherin clears from the apical surface during enteroblast integration.
source: Cadherin clears from the apical surface and an apical space appears between above the enteroblast.
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing E-cadherin localization during different stages of integration (Figure 4).

claim: An apical space appears above the enteroblast during integration.
source: Cadherin clears from the apical surface and an apical space appears between above the enteroblast.
evidence: This is observed in imaging data showing membrane separation (Figures 2, 3).

claim: New septate junctions form laterally between the enteroblast and enterocytes.
source: New septate junctions then form laterally with the enterocytes and the AMIS develops into an apical domain below the enterocyte septate junction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of septate junction markers like Coracle, Mesh, and Tsp2a during integration (Figures 3, 4).

claim: The AMIS develops into an apical domain below the enterocyte septate junction.
source: New septate junctions then form laterally with the enterocytes and the AMIS develops into an apical domain below the enterocyte septate junction.
evidence: This is shown through sequential imaging of actin and apical markers (Figures 2, 3).

claim: The enteroblast forms a pre-assembled apical compartment before it has a free apical surface in contact with the gut lumen.
source: The enteroblast therefore forms a pre-assembled apical compartment before it has a free apical surface in contact with the gut lumen.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging showing the PAC forms below the existing septate junction (Figure 2G-I).

claim: The enterocyte septate junction disassembles to allow the enteroblast/pre-enterocyte to reach the gut lumen.
source: Finally, the enterocyte septate junction disassembles and the enteroblast/pre-enterocyte reaches the gut lumen with a fully formed brush border.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing cells with closed lumens (septate junction present above) versus open lumens (septate junction absent above) (Figure 2G-I).

claim: The enteroblast/pre-enterocyte reaches the gut lumen with a fully formed brush border.
source: Finally, the enterocyte septate junction disassembles and the enteroblast/pre-enterocyte reaches the gut lumen with a fully formed brush border.
evidence: This is shown by imaging of actin markers and EM showing brush border microvilli in the PAC (Figures 2, 3).

claim: The process of enteroblast integration resembles lumen formation in mammalian epithelial cysts.
source: The process of enteroblast integration resembles lumen formation in mammalian epithelial cysts, highlighting the similarities between the fly midgut and mammalian epithelia.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: The Drosophila midgut functions to absorb nutrients and acts as a barrier to pathogens.
source: Like the mammalian gut, the Drosophila midgut functions to absorb nutrients and acts as a barrier to pathogens (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The adult midgut consists of a single layer of polarised epithelial cells, with their apical sides facing the gut lumen and basal sides contacting the extracellular matrix (ECM) and muscle layer.
source: The adult midgut consists of a single layer of polarised epithelial cells, with their apical sides facing the gut lumen and basal sides contacting the extracellular matrix (ECM) and muscle layer (Baumann, 2001; Chen et al., 2018; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The epithelium is predominantly composed of enterocytes (90%).
source: The epithelium is predominantly composed of enterocytes (90%) and also contains entero-endocrine cells (ee) and their progenitors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about midgut composition.

claim: The intestinal stem cells (ISCs) and their progeny, the enteroblasts reside on the basal side of the epithelium beneath the enterocytes.
source: The intestinal stem cells (ISCs) and their progeny, the enteroblasts reside on the basal side of the epithelium beneath the enterocytes (Goulas et al., 2012; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Quiescent enteroblasts are morphologically indistinguishable from ISCs until they are activated to differentiate in response to damage or nutrient-dependent signals.
source: Quiescent enteroblasts are morphologically indistinguishable from ISCs until they are activated to differentiate in response to damage or nutrient-dependent signals (Nászai et al., 2015; O'Brien et al., 2011; Rojas Villa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Multiple signaling pathways have been found to control ISC proliferation and differentiation over the past 15 years.
source: Over the past 15 years, multiple signaling pathways have been found to control ISC proliferation and differentiation, but much less is known about how differentiating enteroblasts insert into the midgut epithelium and polarize to form an apical domain (Antonello et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; He et al., 2018; Jiang and Edgar, 2011; Sasaki et al., 2021; Wang and Hou, 2010; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Much less is known about how differentiating enteroblasts insert into the midgut epithelium and polarize to form an apical domain.
source: Over the past 15 years, multiple signaling pathways have been found to control ISC proliferation and differentiation, but much less is known about how differentiating enteroblasts insert into the midgut epithelium and polarize to form an apical domain (Antonello et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; He et al., 2018; Jiang and Edgar, 2011; Sasaki et al., 2021; Wang and Hou, 2010; Wu et al., 2021).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The adult midgut epithelium is a secondary epithelium that is derived from the endoderm.
source: Firstly, it is a secondary epithelium that is derived from the endoderm, in contrast to most Drosophila epithelia which are directly descend from the cellular blastoderm epithelium (Pitsidianaki et al., 2021; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994a; Yarnitzky and Volk, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most Drosophila epithelia directly descend from the cellular blastoderm epithelium.
source: Firstly, it is a secondary epithelium that is derived from the endoderm, in contrast to most Drosophila epithelia which are directly descend from the cellular blastoderm epithelium (Pitsidianaki et al., 2021; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994a; Yarnitzky and Volk, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The apical-basal polarity of the midgut epithelium does not require the conserved epithelial polarity factors that polarize all ectodermal and mesodermal epithelia.
source: Secondly, the apical-basal polarity of the epithelium does not require the conserved epithelial polarity factors that polarize all ectodermal and mesodermal epithelia, although most of these factors are expressed in the midgut.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The polarity of the midgut enterocytes depends on the interaction between the integrin adhesion complex and the basement membrane.
source: Instead, the polarity of the midgut enterocytes depends on the interaction between the integrin adhesion complex and the basement membrane (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The midgut cells polarise in a basal to apical direction as enteroblasts differentiate into enterocytes as they integrate from the basal side.
source: Thirdly, the midgut cells polarise in a basal to apical direction as enteroblasts differentiate into enterocytes as they integrate from the basal side.
evidence: This is a key observation from the current study.

claim: Other well-characterised Drosophila epithelia, such as the cellular blastoderm and the follicular epithelium form in an apical to basal direction.
source: By contrast, the other well-characterised Drosophila epithelia, such as the cellular blastoderm and the follicular epithelium form in an apical to basal direction (Franz and Riechmann, 2010; Müller, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The midgut epithelium has an inverted arrangement of lateral junctions to other Drosophila epithelia.
source: Finally, the midgut epithelium has an inverted arrangement of lateral junctions to other Drosophila epithelia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about midgut structure.

claim: The occluding, smooth septate junctions form at the top of the lateral domain above typical adherens junctions in the midgut.
source: The occluding, smooth septate junctions, form at the top of the lateral domain above typical adherens junctions, containing E-cadherin (Ecad), α-catenin and Armadillo (β-catenin; Baumann, 2001; Lane and Skaer, 1980; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994a; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The smooth septate junctions are composed of the transmembrane proteins Mesh, Snakeskin (Ssk), Tsp2a and Hoka and the scaffolding protein, Coracle (Cora).
source: The smooth septate junctions are composed of the transmembrane proteins Mesh, Snakeskin (Ssk), Tsp2a and Hoka and the scaffolding protein, Coracle (Cora), and provide the barrier to paracellular diffusion (Furuse and Izumi, 2017; Izumi et al., 2021; Izumi et al., 2016; Izumi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Smooth septate junctions provide the barrier to paracellular diffusion.
source: The smooth septate junctions are composed of the transmembrane proteins Mesh, Snakeskin (Ssk), Tsp2a and Hoka and the scaffolding protein, Coracle (Cora), and provide the barrier to paracellular diffusion (Furuse and Izumi, 2017; Izumi et al., 2021; Izumi et al., 2016; Izumi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ISCs and early enteroblasts lie below the septate junctions between the enterocytes and only form adherens junctions with neighbouring cells.
source: The ISCs and early enteroblasts lie below the septate junctions between the enterocytes and only form adherens junctions with neighbouring cells, while mature enterocytes form both adherens junctions and septate junctions, as well as specialised tri-cellular junctions at the vertex between three cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Mature enterocytes form both adherens junctions and septate junctions, as well as specialised tri-cellular junctions at the vertex between three cells.
source: The ISCs and early enteroblasts lie below the septate junctions between the enterocytes and only form adherens junctions with neighbouring cells, while mature enterocytes form both adherens junctions and septate junctions, as well as specialised tri-cellular junctions at the vertex between three cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data throughout the manuscript.

claim: As an enteroblast differentiates, it needs to develop new septate junctions with the neighbouring enterocytes as it inserts into the epithelium.
source: As an enteroblast differentiates, it therefore needs to develop new septate junctions with the neighbouring enterocytes as it inserts into the epithelium.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structural requirements of integration.

claim: The existing septate junctions between neighbouring enterocytes must be broken to allow the new cell to integrate.
source: This also means that the existing septate junctions between neighbouring enterocytes must be broken to allow the new cell to integrate.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structural requirements of integration.

claim: The barrier function of the epithelium must be maintained during enteroblast integration to prevent the contents of the gut lumen from leaking into the body.
source: Furthermore, the barrier function of the epithelium must be maintained during this process to prevent the contents of the gut lumen, such as digestive enzymes and potential pathogens, from leaking into the body.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional requirement during integration.

claim: In fast radial intercalation, cells form the apical junction and apical domain at the same time, with the apical domain specified after the cells have reached the lumen.
source: In the Xenopus embryonic epidermis and Drosophila renal tubules, progenitor cells and Stellate cells integrate into the outer layer through a process of a fast radial intercalation, in which they form the apical junction and apical domain at the same time. The apical domain is then specified after the cells have reached the lumen (Campbell et al., 2010; Sedzinski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After the first division in MDCK cell cysts, the new membrane between the two daughter cells forms a structure called the AMIS (apical membrane initiation site).
source: After the first division, the new membrane between the two daughter cells forms a structure called the AMIS (apical membrane initiation site), where apical proteins and fluids are secreted to create the lumen (Bryant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the AMIS of MDCK cells, apical proteins and fluids are secreted to create the lumen.
source: After the first division, the new membrane between the two daughter cells forms a structure called the AMIS (apical membrane initiation site), where apical proteins and fluids are secreted to create the lumen (Bryant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In most cells, AMIS formation depends on components of the midbody that forms during cytokinesis and on the development of tight junctions at the lateral margins of the cell contact region.
source: In most cells, AMIS formation depends on components of the midbody that forms during cytokinesis and on the development of tight junctions at the lateral margins of the cell contact region (Blasky et al., 2015; Mangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The site of apical domain formation in inserting enteroblasts cannot be induced by the midbody, since the ISCs divide beneath the epithelial cell layer and the enteroblasts are post-mitotic when they integrate.
source: The site of apical domain formation in inserting enteroblasts cannot be induced by the midbody, however, since the ISCs divide beneath the epithelial cell layer and the enteroblasts are post-mitotic when they integrate.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the spatial and temporal separation of division and integration.

claim: ISCs and early enteroblasts are polarised and localise Par-6 in a crescent at the apex of the cell.
source: Both cell-types are already polarised, as they localise the apical polarity factor Par-6 in a crescent at the apex of the cell (Figure 1A–B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data showing Par-6 localization in Figure 1.

claim: Par-6 is not required for enterocyte polarity.
source: Par-6 is not required for enterocyte polarity, but nonetheless provides a useful marker for the early polarization (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton is not polarised in ISCs and early enteroblasts.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is not polarised at this stage, however, and adherens junctions with the neighbouring enterocytes localize uniformly around the cell (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Adherens junctions with the neighbouring enterocytes localize uniformly around ISCs and early enteroblasts.
source: The actin cytoskeleton is not polarised at this stage, however, and adherens junctions with the neighbouring enterocytes localize uniformly around the cell (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: Canoe is a scaffolding protein that often links the actin cytoskeleton with junctional complexes.
source: Canoe is a scaffolding protein that often links the actin cytoskeleton with junctional complexes (Boettner et al., 2003; Perez-Vale et al., 2021; Sawyer et al., 2009; Yu and Zallen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Canoe localises to the most apical tip of the septate junctions in differentiated enterocytes, forming a thin belt separating the apical brush border from the lateral junctions.
source: Canoe localises to the most apical tip of the septate junctions in differentiated enterocytes, forming a thin belt separating the apical brush border (BB) from the lateral junctions (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The location of Canoe in enterocytes is equivalent to the marginal zone in other fly epithelia and the vertebrate marginal zone (VMZ) in mammalian epithelial cells.
source: This location is equivalent to the marginal zone in other fly epithelia and the vertebrate marginal zone (VMZ) in mammalian epithelial cells (Tan et al., 2020; Tepass, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Canoe localises apically in ISCs and early enteroblasts, which have no septate junctions.
source: Like Par-6, Canoe also localises apically in ISCs and early enteroblasts, which have no septate junctions (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1.

claim: The apical localisation of Canoe and Par6 in ISC/early enteroblasts indicates that they have some apical-basal polarity.
source: The apical localisation of Canoe and Par6 in ISC/early enteroblasts indicates that they have some apical-basal polarity.
evidence: This is an inference from the localization data.

claim: The basal ISCs are found as single cells or as pairs of cells, which can either be two ISCs or an ISC and an enteroblast.
source: The basal ISCs are found as single cells or as pairs of cells, which can either be two ISCs or an ISC and an enteroblast (de Navascués et al., 2012; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ISC/early enteroblasts usually lie underneath the tri-cellular junctions (TCJ) between enterocytes rather than bi-cellular junctions (BCJ).
source: Imaging ECad-GFP flies from the basal side reveals that the ISC/early enteroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) usually lie underneath the tri-cellular junctions (TCJ) between enterocytes rather than bi-cellular junctions (BCJ) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative imaging data in Figure 1E.

claim: Most ISCs/early enteroblasts localise beneath tricellular junctions where three enterocytes meet, whereas entero-endocrine cells mainly lie beneath bicellular junctions.
source: Most ISCs/EBs localise beneath tricellular junctions where three enterocytes meet, whereas entero-endocrine cells mainly lie beneath bicellular junctions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 1E showing 390 ISC/early enteroblasts and 141 ee were scored in 6 guts.

claim: ISCs/early enteroblasts sit immediately beneath the TCJs, marked by Anakonda-GFP.
source: In a side view of the epithelial layer, the ISCs/early enteroblasts sit immediately beneath the TCJs, marked by Anakonda-GFP (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 1F.

claim: Enteroblasts need to break through three mature enterocyte-enterocyte septate junctions to integrate into the epithelial layer and gain access to the gut lumen.
source: This means that enteroblasts need to break through three mature enterocyte-enterocyte septate junctions to integrate into the epithelial layer and gain access to the gut lumen.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that enteroblasts lie beneath tricellular junctions.

claim: Early enteroblasts express the Notch signalling reporter, Su(H)GBE-Gal4 >mCD8 GFP, but this is turned off as they differentiate.
source: Early enteroblasts express the Notch signalling reporter, Su(H)GBE-Gal4 >mCD8 GFP, but this is turned off as they differentiate (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007; Rojas Villa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Enteroblasts that have just started to differentiate can be identified as cells with larger nuclei, in which some GFP signal still perdures.
source: Enteroblasts that have just started to differentiate can therefore be identified as cells with larger nuclei, in which some GFP signal still perdures.
evidence: This is a methodological inference based on the reporter system.

claim: The frequency of early differentiating enteroblasts is very low under homeostatic conditions.
source: The frequency of such early differentiating enteroblasts is very low under homeostatic conditions (Reiff et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Exposure to a 2 hr heat shock at 37 °C increases the number of dividing ISCs and differentiating enteroblasts.
source: We therefore exposed the flies to a 2 hr heat shock at 37 °C to induce minor damage and dissected them 1 day later, which increases the number of dividing ISCs and differentiating Su(H)GBE >mCD8 GFP positive enteroblasts with larger nuclear volumes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Heat shock treatment causes a small increase in Tor kinase activity at the very anterior and posterior ends of the midgut as shown by phospho-4E-BP1 staining.
source: This treatment causes a small increase in Tor kinase activity at the very anterior and posterior ends of the midgut as shown by phospho-4E-BP1 staining, but does not increase pERK staining, an indicator of EGFR/MAPK signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Heat shock treatment does not increase pERK staining, an indicator of EGFR/MAPK signaling.
source: This treatment causes a small increase in Tor kinase activity at the very anterior and posterior ends of the midgut as shown by phospho-4E-BP1 staining, but does not increase pERK staining, an indicator of EGFR/MAPK signaling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The heat shock induces sufficient stress to trigger ISC divisions and enteroblast activation/differentiation but does not activate a regeneration process.
source: Thus, the heat shock induces sufficient stress to trigger ISC divisions and enteroblast activation/differentiation but does not activate a regeneration process.
evidence: This is an inference from the pERK and p4EBP1 data.

claim: A proportion of the differentiating enteroblasts form a 'bubble' like structure inside the epithelial layer.
source: A proportion of the Su(H)GBE >GFP positive, differentiating enteroblasts and the older GFP-negative enteroblasts form a "bubble" like structure inside the epithelial layer (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2A.

claim: The 'bubble' structure is surrounded by membranes, as shown by the localisation of the membrane associated protein, α-Spectrin.
source: This structure is surrounded by membranes, as shown by the localisation of the membrane associated protein, α-Spectrin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2A.

claim: The actin marker sqh::Utrophin actin binding domain-GFP (sqh::Utr-ABD-GFP) localises to the lower portion of the 'bubble'.
source: The actin marker sqh::Utrophin actin binding domain-GFP (sqh::Utr-ABD-GFP), which labels the brush border of mature enterocytes, also localises to the lower portion of the "bubble" (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data.

claim: The actin-rich portion of the 'bubble' is labeled by all apical domain markers examined, including Par-6, Myosin IA, Myosin 7a, Fimbrin, Cheerio, Rab11, and Picot.
source: Furthermore, the actin-rich portion of the 'bubble' is labeled by all other apical domain markers that we have examined, including Par-6, Myosin IA, Myosin 7a, the actin cross-linking proteins, Fimbrin and Cheerio (Lcp1/Pls3 and Filamin in mammals), Rab11, a marker for the apical recycling endosome and Picot, a transmembrane protein with homology to anion co-transporter proteins (Figure 2B–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2B-E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and G.

claim: The lower portion of the 'bubble' corresponds to a nascent apical domain.
source: This strongly suggests that the lower portion of the 'bubble' corresponds to a nascent apical domain.
evidence: This is an inference from the marker localization data.

claim: EM images reveal that the lower part of the 'bubble' structure forms a brush border.
source: In support of this view, EM images reveal that this region forms a brush border (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 2F.

claim: The lower part of the 'bubble' structure has all the features of a pre-assembled apical domain, although it is not at the apical side of the epithelium.
source: Thus, the lower part of the 'bubble' structure has all the features of a pre-assembled apical domain, although it is not at the apical side of the epithelium.
evidence: This is an inference from the combined marker and EM data.

claim: Only the integrating enteroblast/pre-enterocyte forms an apical domain in the fly midgut, whereas mammalian epithelial cysts are symmetric with cells on both sides of the lumen forming apical domains.
source: Another important difference between the two systems is that mammalian epithelial cysts are symmetric, with the cells on both sides of the lumen forming apical domains, whereas only the integrating enteroblast/pre-enterocyte forms an apical domain in the fly midgut.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis based on the authors' observations and previous literature.

claim: The overlying enterocytes do not form a normal lateral domain over the lumen, as βH-Spectrin and Canoe localise to the enterocyte cortex in this region.
source: The overlying enterocytes do not form a normal lateral domain over the lumen, however, as βH-Spectrin and Canoe localise to the enterocyte cortex in this region, which is quite different to their localisations in mature enterocytes to the apical domain and the marginal zone above the septate junctions, respectively.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data showing Canoe localization (Figure 7A).

claim: In most cases, the internal apical domain lay beneath the septate junction connecting the overlying enterocytes, indicating that the lumen lies within the epithelium and does not connect to the gut lumen.
source: In most cases, the internal apical domain lay beneath the septate junction connecting the overlying enterocytes, indicating that the lumen lies within the epithelium and does not connect to the gut lumen (Figure 2G and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2G and I.

claim: In some cases, the only septate junctions are the new junctions between the invaginating enteroblast and the neighbouring enterocytes and the lumen is continuous with the gut lumen.
source: In other cases, the only septate junctions are the new junctions between the invaginating enteroblast and the neighbouring enterocytes and the lumen is continuous with the gut lumen (Figure 2H and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 2H and I.

claim: The enteroblasts first form an apical domain and lumen within the epithelium, then the septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes disappears, allowing the internal lumen to fuse with the gut lumen.
source: Thus, the enteroblasts first form an apical domain and lumen within the epithelium. The septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes then disappears, allowing the internal lumen to fuse with the gut lumen and the apical domain to reach the apical surface.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing cells at different stages.

claim: In the 'closed' PAC stage, a new set of septate junctions form beneath the septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes.
source: In the 'closed' PAC stage, when the PAC is not exposed to the gut lumen, a new set of septate junctions form beneath the septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of septate junction markers (Figures 2, 3).

claim: The pre-enterocyte has septate junctions with its neighbours and a fully-developed apical brush border before it emerges on the apical surface, thereby maintaining the gut barrier during enteroblast integration.
source: This means that the pre-enterocyte has septate junctions with its neighbours and a fully-developed apical brush border before it emerges on the apical surface, thereby maintaining the gut barrier during enteroblast integration (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an inference from the sequential stages observed.

claim: Actin is diffusely distributed around the cell cortex in the first stage of PAC formation, while Canoe and Cora are enriched apically.
source: In the first stage, actin is diffusely distributed around the cell cortex, as it is in quiescent enteroblasts, but Canoe and Cora enriched apically (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: Actin becomes enriched apically in a slightly smaller domain than Canoe and Cora during AMIS formation.
source: Actin then becomes enriched apically in a slightly smaller domain than Canoe and Cora (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3B.

claim: The co-localisation of actin and junctional proteins during AMIS formation is reminiscent of the apical membrane initiation site (AMIS) in MDCK cells.
source: This co-localisation of actin and junctional proteins is reminiscent of the apical membrane initiation site (AMIS) in MDCK cells (Bryant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Coincident with the apical enrichment of actin, a slight separation appears between the apical membrane of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocyte membranes, suggesting that fluid is being secreted into this space.
source: Coincident with the apical enrichment of actin, a slight separation appears between the apical membrane of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocyte membranes, suggesting that fluid is being secreted into this space (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3B, with the suggestion of fluid secretion being an inference.

claim: The actin staining becomes concentrated in the centre of the apical domain, while Canoe and Cora are depleted from this region, creating a central actin-rich zone that lacks junctional proteins.
source: The actin staining then becomes concentrated in the centre of the apical domain, while Canoe and Cora are depleted from this region, creating a central actin-rich zone that lacks junctional proteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3C.

claim: The small actin region expands, bends inwards and becomes the PAC, whereas Cora localises to the newly-forming septate junctions on either side.
source: This small actin region then expands, bends inwards and becomes the PAC, whereas Cora localises to the newly-forming septate junctions on either side, with Canoe slightly more apical in the nascent marginal zone (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3D.

claim: The pre-existing septate junction above the PAC disappears, and the PAC everts to form the apical domain.
source: Finally, the pre-existing septate junction above the PAC disappears, and the PAC everts to form the apical domain (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3E.

claim: Early enteroblasts that have not reached the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes form adherens junctions with the adjacent enterocytes all round their contacting surfaces.
source: Early enteroblasts that have not reached the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes form adherens junctions (AJ) with the adjacent enterocytes all round their contacting surfaces (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4A.

claim: Canoe and Cora become polarised apically when the integrating enteroblast contacts the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction above, but the adherens junctions remain uniformly distributed.
source: Canoe and Cora become polarised apically when the integrating enteroblast contacts the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction above, but the adherens junctions remain uniformly distributed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4B.

claim: As actin and Canoe become enriched apically to form the AMIS, adherens junctions are lost from this region and the enteroblast membrane separates from the membranes of the overlying enterocytes.
source: As actin and Canoe become enriched apically to form the AMIS, adherens junctions are lost from this region and the enteroblast membrane separates from the membranes of the overlying enterocytes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4C.

claim: Adherens junctions remain absent from the AMIS region as the PAC starts to form.
source: Adherens junctions remain absent from this region as the PAC starts to form (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4D.

claim: AMIS formation is associated with the loss of adherens junctions, which is presumably required to allow the enteroblast membrane to separate from that of the overlying enterocytes.
source: Thus, AMIS formation is associated with the loss of adherens junctions. This is presumably required to allow the enteroblast membrane to separate from that of the overlying enterocytes, as fluid is secreted from the AMIS to form the internal lumen.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed loss of adherens junctions.

claim: The transcription factor Sox21a is required for the differentiation of enteroblasts into enterocytes.
source: The transcription factor Sox21a is required for the differentiation of enteroblasts into enterocytes and can induce the precocious differentiation of quiescent enteroblasts when over-expressed, in part by activating the expression of another transcription factor, Pdm1 (Chen et al., 2016; Meng and Biteau, 2015; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sox21a can induce the precocious differentiation of quiescent enteroblasts when over-expressed, in part by activating the expression of Pdm1.
source: The transcription factor Sox21a is required for the differentiation of enteroblasts into enterocytes and can induce the precocious differentiation of quiescent enteroblasts when over-expressed, in part by activating the expression of another transcription factor, Pdm1 (Chen et al., 2016; Meng and Biteau, 2015; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nuclear Sox21a is present at high levels in unpolarised enteroblasts, but the levels are significantly lower in polarised enteroblasts.
source: Nuclear Sox21a is present at high levels in unpolarised enteroblasts, which probably correspond to the oval-shaped enteroblasts described by Chen et al., 2016, but the levels are significantly lower in polarised enteroblasts (Figure 5A, B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative imaging data in Figure 5A, B and D.

claim: Sox21a is no longer detectable above background in the nuclei of pre-enterocytes that have formed a PAC.
source: Sox21a is no longer detectable above background in the nuclei of pre-enterocytes that have formed a PAC, with a nuclear intensity similar to that in the neighbouring Sox21a-negative enterocytes (Figure 5B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative imaging data in Figure 5B and D.

claim: Pre-enterocytes are similar to enterocytes at the transcriptional level, as they express the enterocyte marker, Pdm1.
source: Indeed, the pre-enterocytes are similar to enterocytes at the transcriptional level, as they also express the enterocyte marker, Pdm1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5C.

claim: Sox21a levels are inversely correlated with enteroblast differentiation and integration.
source: Sox21a levels are therefore inversely correlated with enteroblast differentiation and integration: unpolarised enteroblasts have high Sox21a, polarised enteroblasts with an AMIS have lower levels, and pre-enterocytes with a PAC are Pdm1 +and Sox21a- like the neighbouring enterocytes (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference from the quantitative data in Figure 5.

claim: Most activated EBs take about 24 hr to develop into a pre-EC with a PAC and a further 24 hr to differentiate into a mature EC after Sox21a induction.
source: Assuming that it takes 12–17 hr to induce high levels of Sox21a expression, these results suggest that most activated EBs take about 24 hr to develop into a pre-EC with a PAC and a further 24 hr to differentiate into a mature EC, although some cells differentiate faster.
evidence: This is an inference from the time course experiment in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: This time frame for enteroblast differentiation is in agreement with a previous study using similar approaches to accelerate differentiation.
source: This time frame is in agreement with a previous study using similar approaches to accelerate differentiation (Rojas Villa et al., 2019) and a recent live imaging study tracing the enteroblast to enterocyte transition (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Down-regulation of Sox21a is not essential for enteroblast to pre-enterocyte differentiation, since enteroblasts overexpressing Sox21a still form a PAC.
source: This experiment also indicates that down-regulation of Sox21a is not essential for enteroblast to pre-enterocyte differentiation, since enteroblasts overexpressing Sox21a still from a PAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When an enteroblast is activated by high Sox21a expression, it starts to grow in size but loses its apical-basal polarity.
source: When an enteroblast is activated by high Sox21a expression, it starts to grow in size but loses its apical-basal polarity, with adherens junctions all over its contacting surface and uniform cortical actin.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the imaging data.

claim: Once the enteroblast reaches the septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes, Canoe and Cora become localised apically.
source: Once the enteroblast reaches the septate junction between the neighbouring enterocytes, Canoe and Cora become localised apically.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The apical membrane initiation site forms with the apical localisation of F-actin and the removal of DE-cadherin from this region, coinciding with the down-regulation of Sox21a.
source: Shortly afterwards, the apical membrane initiation site forms, with the apical localisation of F-actin and the removal of DE-cadherin from this region. This coincides with the down-regulation of Sox21a and the opening of a space between the plasma membranes of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocytes, suggesting that the apical membrane is secreting fluid between the cells.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the imaging data in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The opening of a space between the plasma membranes of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocytes suggests that the apical membrane is secreting fluid between the cells.
source: Shortly afterwards, the apical membrane initiation site forms, with the apical localisation of F-actin and the removal of DE-cadherin from this region. This coincides with the down-regulation of Sox21a and the opening of a space between the plasma membranes of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocytes, suggesting that the apical membrane is secreting fluid between the cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed membrane separation.

claim: As the cell differentiates into a pre-enterocyte, F-actin segregates from Canoe and Coracle into the centre of the AMIS to form the nascent PAC.
source: As the cell differentiates into a pre-enterocyte, F-actin segregates from Canoe and Coracle into the centre of the AMIS to form the nascent PAC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: The PAC expands and new septate junctions marked by Cora, Mesh and Tsp2A form between the enteroblast and the adjacent enterocytes, sealing the fluid-filled lumen above the PAC.
source: The PAC then expands and new septate junctions marked by Cora, Mesh (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) and Tsp2A (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) form between the enteroblast and the adjacent enterocytes, sealing the fluid-filled lumen above the PAC.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: By the stage when new septate junctions form, the pre-enterocyte no longer expresses Sox21a and has activated Pdm1.
source: By this stage, the pre-enterocyte no longer expresses Sox21a and has activated Pdm1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 5.

claim: The septate junctions above the internal lumen disassemble, allowing the membranes of the overlying enterocytes to separate, so that the lumen becomes continuous with the gut lumen.
source: Finally, the septate junctions above the internal lumen disassemble, allowing the membranes of the overlying enterocytes to separate, so that the lumen becomes continuous with the gut lumen.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing cells with closed versus open lumens.

claim: At the point when the lumen becomes continuous with the gut lumen, the PAC becomes the apical domain of the newly-integrated enterocyte.
source: At this point the PAC becomes the apical domain of the newly-integrated enterocyte (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is a summary of the integration process.

claim: The mechanisms that drive the disassembly of the overlying septate junctions are not known.
source: The mechanisms that drive the disassembly of the overlying septate junctions are not known, but it is worth bearing in mind that most EBs integrate beneath a tricellular junction.
evidence: This acknowledges a gap in understanding.

claim: Most EBs integrate beneath a tricellular junction, which must be disassembled to allow the new enterocyte to emerge on the apical surface.
source: The mechanisms that drive the disassembly of the overlying septate junctions are not known, but it is worth bearing in mind that most EBs integrate beneath a tricellular junction. This tricellular junction must therefore also be disassembled to allow the new enterocyte to emerge on the apical surface, and three new tricellular junctions must eventually form where the new enterocyte meets two of the adjacent enterocytes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation that EBs integrate beneath tricellular junctions.

claim: The disassembly of the overlying tricellular junction may be the first event that triggers the emergence of the new enterocyte.
source: Indeed, the disassembly of the overlying tricellular junction may be the first event that triggers the emergence of the new enterocyte (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Canoe localises to the enterocyte membranes that separate from the apical membrane of the enteroblast and cover the internal lumen during AMIS and PAC formation.
source: During AMIS and PAC formation, we noticed that Canoe also localises to the enterocyte membranes that separate from the apical membrane of the enteroblast and cover the internal lumen (orange arrow in Figure 4C, yellow arrow in Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 4C and 7A.

claim: Enterocytes respond to the presence of an invaginating enteroblast/pre-enterocyte by re-localising Canoe.
source: Since Canoe normally localises to the marginal zone above the septate junctions in enterocytes, this suggests that enterocytes respond to the presence of an invaginating enteroblast/pre-enterocyte by re-localising Canoe.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed Canoe localization.

claim: When one of the adjacent enterocytes is mutant for canoe, Canoe is lost from the enterocyte membrane covering that side of the internal lumen.
source: When one of the adjacent enterocytes is mutant for canoe, Canoe is lost from the enterocyte membrane covering that side of the internal lumen, confirming that this signal normally comes from the enterocyte (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7B using MARCM clones.

claim: When the pre-enterocyte is mutant for canoe, staining is lost from the bottom surface of the PAC.
source: Consistent with this, when the pre-enterocyte is mutant for canoe, staining is lost from the bottom surface of the PAC (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7C.

claim: The PAC forms normally in canoe mutant cells, suggesting that Canoe is not required for enteroblast integration or polarisation.
source: In both cases, however, the PAC forms normally, suggesting that Canoe is not required for enteroblast integration or polarisation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that canoe mutant cells still form PACs.

claim: MARCM clones of the canoejc allele lack Canoe staining, but are otherwise wild-type, confirming that Canoe is not required for enteroblast integration or enterocyte polarity.
source: MARCM clones of this allele, canoejc, lack Canoe staining, but are otherwise wild-type, confirming that Canoe is not required for enteroblast integration or enterocyte polarity (Figure 7D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7D-E.

claim: Coracle is a peripheral septate junction protein whose localisation depends on the structural septate junction components such as Mesh/Ssk/Tsp2a.
source: Coracle is a peripheral septate junction protein whose localisation depends on the structural septate junction components such as Mesh/Ssk/Tsp2a (Chen et al., 2018; Izumi et al., 2016; Izumi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells mutant for corajc or cora5 can form a PAC, septate junctions and a full apical domain, indicating that Cora is not required for enteroblast integration or enterocyte polarity.
source: Cells mutant for this allele, corajc, or a second cora null allele, cora5, can form a PAC, septate junctions and a full apical domain, indicating that Cora is also not required for enteroblast integration or enterocyte polarity (Figure 7F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The smooth septate junctions of the Drosophila midgut are formed by several transmembrane proteins, including Mesh, Tsp2A and Snakeskin (Ssk), which are specifically expressed in endodermal tissues.
source: The smooth septate junctions of the Drosophila midgut are formed by several transmembrane proteins, including Mesh, Tsp2A and Snakeskin (Ssk), which are specifically expressed in endodermal tissues (Furuse and Izumi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: meshR2 and meshf04955 homozygous cells never integrate fully into the epithelial layer and remain below the septate junctions of the overlying enterocytes.
source: meshR2 and meshf04955 homozygous cells never integrate fully into the epithelial layer and remain below the septate junctions of the overlying enterocytes, presumably because they cannot make septate junctions of their own (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8A-C.

claim: mesh mutant cells accumulate in the basal region of the epithelium, with new EBs derived from the same mutant ISC forming beneath them and reducing their contact with the basement membrane.
source: Because the mutant cells remain trapped beneath enterocyte-enterocyte septate junctions, they accumulate in the basal region of the epithelium, with new EBs derived from the same mutant ISC forming beneath them and reducing their contact with the basement membrane (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8A.

claim: Some mesh mutant cells contain one or more circular, actin-rich structures that are labelled by α-Spectrin and the apical domain proteins, Par-6, Myo7a and Rab11.
source: Some of the mesh mutant cells contain one or more circular, actin-rich structures that are labelled by α-Spectrin and the apical domain proteins, Par-6, Myo7a and Rab11 (Figure 8C, E, G and H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8C, E, G and H.

claim: The circular, actin-rich structures in mesh mutant cells resemble PACs, but do not face the external space between the enteroblast and enterocytes, instead forming inside the cells.
source: These structures resemble PACs, but do not face the external space between the enteroblast and enterocytes, instead forming inside the cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the imaging data.

claim: Cells with an internal PAC account for 12% of the meshR2 enteroblasts.
source: Cells with an internal PAC account for 12% of the meshR2 enteroblasts.
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells.

claim: 81% of differentiating mesh mutant enteroblasts do not appear to be polarised, with actin and βH-Spectrin diffusely distributed around the contacting cell surface.
source: 81% of differentiating mesh mutant enteroblasts, based on their size and ploidy (>8 n), do not appear to be polarised, with actin and βH-Spectrin diffusely distributed around the contacting cell surface (Figure 8D and J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: 7% of mesh mutant enteroblasts are polarised, with actin, Par-6 and Rab11 localised apically.
source: The remaining mutant cells (7%) are polarised, with actin, Par-6 and Rab11 localised apically (Figure 8E, F and J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Mutants in other septate junction proteins also disrupt PAC formation, but cause a lower frequency of internal PACs than mesh mutants.
source: Mutants in other septate junction proteins also disrupt PAC formation, but cause a lower frequency of internal PACs.
evidence: This is a summary of quantitative data in Figure 8J.

claim: Only 0.6% Tsp2a mutant cells have an internal PAC and 11% still polarise, with the rest showing little or no sign of polarity.
source: Only 0.6% Tsp2a mutant cells have an internal PAC and 11% still polarise, with the rest showing little or no sign of polarity (Figure 8J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, F, K and L).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: 0.5% of ssk mutant cells form an internal PAC, 17% polarise and 78.6% do not polarise.
source: Similarly 0.5% of ssk mutant cells form an internal PAC, 17% polarise and 78.6% do not polarise (Figure 8J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: A small fraction of ssk mutant cells form a normal PAC (1.3%) and even integrate into the epithelial layer (2.6%).
source: However, a small fraction of ssk mutant cells form a normal PAC (1.3%) and even integrate into the epithelial layer (2.6%) (Figure 8J, Figure 8—figure supplement 1G and J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting mutant cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: More than 80% of the cells in control FRT82B MARCM clones develop a mature apical domain, while the remaining ~10% lack apical actin and are presumably ISCs or early enteroblasts.
source: By contrast, more than 80% of the cells in control FRT82B MARCM clones develop a mature apical domain, while the remaining ~10% lack apical actin and are presumably ISCs or early enteroblasts (Figure 8J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from counting control cells, shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Mutants in each septate junction protein disrupt the localisation of the other septate junction components.
source: Mutants in each septate junction protein disrupt the localisation of the other septate junction components, as previously reported for the embryonic and larval gut (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C; Izumi et al., 2021; Izumi et al., 2016; Izumi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C and supported by citations.

claim: The differences between the spectrums of phenotypes observed in mesh, Tsp2a and ssk mutants cannot be explained by their distinct effects on septate junction formation and may reflect differences in perdurance or other functions of these proteins.
source: The differences between the spectrums of phenotypes observed in mesh, Tsp2a and ssk mutants therefore cannot be explained by their distinct effects on septate junction formation and may reflect differences in perdurance or other functions of these proteins, such as the regulation of the Yki pathway (Chen et al., 2020; Izumi et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about the reasons for phenotypic differences, with citations to other functions.

claim: The majority of cells mutant for septate junction components fail to polarise or form an AMIS, although they form normal lateral and basal domains.
source: The majority of cells mutant for septate junction components fail to polarise or form an AMIS, although they form normal lateral and basal domains, as shown by the normal localisation of the basal integrin signalling component, Talin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1N.

claim: The initial apical-basal polarisation of ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts is not affected in mesh, Tsp2a and ssk mutant clones.
source: This contrasts with the initial apical-basal polarisation of ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts, which are not affected in mesh, Tsp2a and ssk mutant clones (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: mesh, Tsp2a and ssk mutant clones have similar sizes to the control empty FRT82B clones, indicating that they have no effect on stem cell behaviour or division rate.
source: The mutant clones also have similar sizes to the control empty FRT82B clones, indicating that they have no effect on stem cell behaviour or division rate (Figure 8—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1O.

claim: The septate junction proteins are not involved in the initial polarisation of ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts, but they are required for the apical-basal polarisation that gives rise to the AMIS in most cells.
source: Thus, the septate junction proteins are not involved in the initial polarisation of ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts, but they are required for the apical-basal polarisation that gives rise to the AMIS in most cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutant phenotypes.

claim: The role of septate junction proteins in AMIS formation is distinct from the role of integrin adhesion complex, which is required for apical-basal polarity in ISCs, quiescent enteroblasts and activated enteroblasts.
source: This is distinct from the role of integrin adhesion complex, which is required for apical-basal polarity in ISCs, quiescent enteroblasts and activated enteroblasts (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F-H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2F-H.

claim: Some mutant enteroblasts still polarise to form an AMIS-like structure in the absence of septate junction proteins, since 5–20% of mutant cells still localise actin, Par-6 and Rab11 apically.
source: Some mutant enteroblasts still polarise to form an AMIS-like structure in the absence of septate junction proteins, since 5–20% of mutant cells still localise actin, Par-6 and Rab11 apically (Arrows in Figure 8E–H), lose their apical Adherens junctions from this region and detach their apical membrane from the overlying wild-type enterocytes (Figure 8D and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 8E-H.

claim: In mesh and Tsp2A mutants, the AMIS-like structure never gives rise to a PAC.
source: In the case of mesh and Tsp2A, this AMIS-like structure never gives rise to a PAC.
evidence: This is an observation from the mutant analysis.

claim: The low frequency of AMIS formation in septate junction mutants may be due to partial rescue of the phenotype by the perdurance of the wild-type proteins after clone induction.
source: The low frequency of AMIS formation in these mutants may be due to partial rescue of the phenotype by the perdurance of the wild-type proteins after clone induction.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for residual AMIS formation.

claim: The formation of the AMIS may not absolutely require the septate junction proteins, but only occur very inefficiently in their absence.
source: Alternatively, the formation of the AMIS may not absolutely require the septate junction proteins, but only occur very inefficiently in their absence.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of septate junction proteins.

claim: Enteroblasts perform an essential role in gut homeostasis by providing a pool of quiescent precursor cells that can rapidly integrate into the epithelium in response to damage or growth signals.
source: Enteroblasts perform an essential role in gut homeostasis by providing a pool of quiescent precursor cells that can rapidly integrate into the epithelium in response to damage or growth signals to replace or increase the number of enterocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about enteroblast function.

claim: Enteroblasts integrate by forming an apical domain inside the epithelial layer, immediately beneath the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes.
source: Our results reveal that they do this by an unexpected mechanism, in which they form an apical domain inside the epithelial layer, immediately beneath the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding from the study.

claim: The enteroblast/pre-enterocyte forms new septate junctions with its neighbours before the septate junctions above the integrating cell are removed, providing an elegant solution to maintaining the barrier during integration.
source: This therefore provides an elegant solution to the problem of integrating into the epithelium without disrupting the barrier, by forming junctions between the enteroblast/pre-enterocyte and its neighbours before the septate junctions above the integrating cell are removed.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the observed mechanism.

claim: The pre-enterocyte already has a fully differentiated apical domain with a brush border when it reaches the gut lumen, so that it can immediately assume its function in nutrient absorption.
source: This also means that the pre-enterocyte already has a fully differentiated apical domain with a brush border when it reaches the gut lumen, so that it can immediately assume its function in nutrient absorption.
evidence: This is an inference about the functional significance of the observed mechanism.

claim: The sequence of events in enteroblast integration has been inferred from ordering images of many fixed samples based on cell size and the localisation of various proteins.
source: This sequence of events has been inferred from ordering images of many fixed samples based on cell size and the localisation of various proteins, but it will be important to corroborate this sequence by imaging enteroblast integration in living midguts.
evidence: This acknowledges the methodological approach and its limitations.

claim: The results are entirely consistent with another recent study of enteroblast integration in the adult midgut, which reached very similar conclusions.
source: Nevertheless, our results are entirely consistent with another recent study of enteroblast integration in the adult midgut, which reached very similar conclusions (Moreno-Roman et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a concurrent study.

claim: Growing enteroblasts go through a phase where they lack a distinct apical domain, in contrast to ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts, which are polarised.
source: This reveals that growing enteroblasts go through a phase where they lack a distinct apical domain, in contrast to ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts, which are polarised and localise Canoe and Par-6 apically.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: Unpolarised enteroblasts are likely to correspond to the protrusive, migratory state of activated enteroblasts reported by Antonella et al.
source: These unpolarised enteroblasts are likely to correspond to the protrusive, migratory state of activated enteroblasts reported by Antonella et al., indicating that growing enteroblasts go through a mesenchymal stage (Antonello et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current observations to previous literature.

claim: Adult enteroblasts transiently lose polarity and become migratory before developing epithelial polarity, much like the embryonic midgut precursors.
source: Thus, the adult enteroblasts transiently lose polarity and become migratory before developing epithelial polarity, much like the embryonic midgut precursors, which undergo an epithelial to mesenchymal transition when they delaminate from the primary epithelium and become migratory, before re-polarising in contact with the visceral mesoderm to form the embryonic midgut epithelium (Campbell et al., 2011; Pitsidianaki et al., 2021; Tepass and Hartenstein, 1994a).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis supported by citations.

claim: The re-polarisation of growing enteroblasts upon reaching the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction occurs in two steps, with Canoe and septate junction proteins appearing at the apical membrane first, followed by F-actin.
source: The re-polarisation of growing enteroblasts upon reaching the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction occurs in two steps, with Canoe and septate junction proteins appearing at the apical membrane first, followed by F-actin.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the imaging data.

claim: The apical localisation of actin coincides with the clearance of adherens junctions from the apical membrane and is followed by the appearance of a space between the apical membrane of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocytes.
source: The apical localisation of actin coincides with the clearance of adherens junctions from the apical membrane and is followed by the appearance of a space between the apical membrane of the enteroblast and the overlying enterocytes.
evidence: This is a summary of observations from the imaging data.

claim: The enteroblast is secreting fluid into the extracellular space between it and the enterocytes to separate the cell membranes.
source: This suggests that the enteroblast is secreting fluid into the extracellular space between it and the enterocytes to separate the cell membranes, which are no longer held together via the E-cadherin adhesion.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed membrane separation.

claim: Fluid secretion may be driven by apical exocytosis of vesicles or the activity of water and ion channels.
source: This may be driven by apical exocytosis of vesicles or the activity of water and ion channels.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of fluid secretion.

claim: The central actin-rich region expands to form the pre-apical compartment and often invaginates inwards, perhaps due to the fluid pressure of the lumen above.
source: The central actin-rich region then expands to form the pre-apical compartment and often invaginates inwards, perhaps due to the fluid pressure of the lumen above.
evidence: This is an observation with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The steps in the formation of the pre-assembled apical compartment bear several similarities with cyst formation in mammalian epithelial cultures in 3D.
source: The steps in the formation of the pre-assembled apical compartment bear several similarities with cyst formation in mammalian epithelial cultures in 3D, which also involves the development of an internal lumen at sites of cell-cell contact.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis.

claim: In MDCK cysts, the first sign of lumen development is the formation of an apical membrane initiation site, which is marked by the co-localisation of tight junction proteins with the apical marker, Podocalyxin.
source: In MDCK cysts, for example, the first sign of lumen development is the formation of an apical membrane initiation site, which is marked by the co-localisation of tight junction proteins, such as Cingulin and Occludin with the apical marker, Podocalyxin (Bryant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The AMIS in MDCK cysts develops into a pre-apical patch as Cingulin and Occludin segregate away from the apical factors to form lateral tight junctions that seal the lumen, mirroring the behaviour of septate junction proteins in Drosophila enteroblasts.
source: The AMIS then develops into a pre-apical patch as Cingulin and Occludin segregate away from the apical factors to form lateral tight junctions that seal the lumen, mirroring the behaviour of septate junction proteins in Drosophila enteroblasts (Blasky et al., 2015; Mangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis supported by citations.

claim: The formation of an internal lumen in MDCK cysts is preceded by the loss of Cadherin from the contacting cell-cell surfaces, as it is in Drosophila enterocytes.
source: Similarly, the formation of an internal lumen in MDCK cysts is preceded by the loss of Cadherin from the contacting cell-cell surfaces, as it is in Drosophila enterocytes (Ferrari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis supported by a citation.

claim: Junctional proteins are required to define the site of apical secretion in both MDCK cysts and Drosophila enteroblasts.
source: Furthermore, junctional proteins are required to define the site of apical secretion in both systems, as knockdown of Cingulin blocks the formation of a single lumen in MDCK cysts and loss of Mesh or Tsp2a prevents the development of an external lumen in the Drosophila midgut (Mangan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis supported by a citation.

claim: The most likely cue for the repolarisation that creates the AMIS in Drosophila enteroblasts is the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes.
source: The most likely cue for the repolarisation that creates the AMIS in Drosophila enteroblasts is the septate junction between the overlying enterocytes, as enteroblasts do not polarise until they reach this junction.
evidence: This is an inference from the observations.

claim: 80–90% of enteroblasts mutant for septate junction components fail to polarise, suggesting that septate junction proteins play a role in sensing when the integrating enteroblast contacts the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction.
source: 80–90% of enteroblasts mutant for septate junction components fail to polarise at this stage, suggesting that septate junction proteins play a role in sensing when the integrating enteroblast contacts the enterocyte-enterocyte septate junction.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutant phenotype data.

claim: The enteroblast does not form three-way septate junctions with the existing septate junctions, because the enteroblast only forms septate junctions later and in a more lateral position.
source: However, this cannot be by forming three-way septate junctions with the existing septate junctions, because the enteroblast only forms septate junctions later and in a more lateral position.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed timing and location of septate junction formation.

claim: The enterocytes must disassemble the septate junction above a pre-enterocyte for the latter to reach the gut lumen.
source: For example, the enterocytes must disassemble the septate junction above a pre-enterocyte for the latter to reach the gut lumen.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observed sequence of events.

claim: The enterocytes receive cues from the invaginating enteroblast that produce specific responses at each stage of the process.
source: This suggests that the enterocytes receive cues from the invaginating enteroblast that produce specific responses at each stage of the process, although the nature of these signals is not known.
evidence: This is speculation about cell-cell communication.

claim: The development of an enterocyte from an ISC involves first the loss of the apical-basal polarity shown by ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts and then the re-establishment of polarity as the AMIS forms.
source: The development of an enterocyte from an ISC involves first the loss of the apical-basal polarity shown by ISCs and quiescent enteroblasts and then the re-establishment of polarity as the AMIS forms.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed developmental sequence.

claim: Differentiating enteroblasts require both a basal cue and a junctional cue to form the AMIS and PAC.
source: Thus, differentiating enteroblasts only require a basal cue to establish their initial apical-basal polarity, whereas the formation of the pre-assembled apical compartment also requires a junctional cue.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutant phenotypes.
